items.prose: A forward-only test scores +1 right and −1 wrong. You answered 66 questions, 9 of them wrong.
items.question: What is your net score?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the right count first.

byKey.right-count: 57 is the right count. Take off 9 for the wrong answers: 48.
byKey.answered: 66 counts every answer as right. 9 were wrong, so $57 - 9 = 48$.

explain.text: 66 answered with 9 wrong leaves 57 right. Net is $57 - 9 = 48$. Each wrong answer cost two marks against a right one.

items.prose: Forward only, +1 right and −1 wrong, four options. A question would take you 24 s. Instead you can remove two options in 3 s and guess. Elsewhere you run at 6 s a question with 80% right.
items.question: If you guess, what do the guess and the questions bought with the 21 s saved earn on average?

widget.label: Average marks
widget.accept: 2.1: 3.5 questions at 0.6, and 0 for the guess.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each question earns $0.8 - 0.2$; 21 s buys 3.5 of them.

byKey.no-penalty: 2.8 counts 0.8 per question. A wrong answer costs a mark, so each earns $0.8 - 0.2 = 0.6$.
byKey.full-time: 2.4 spends all 24 s on new questions. The guess itself takes 3 s, leaving 21.
byKey.solve: 0.6 is what solving the slow question earns. The trade earns 2.1.

explain.text: A guess among two averages 0, and 21 s buys 3.5 questions at 6 s. Each earns $0.8 - 0.2 = 0.6$, so 2.1 in all. Solving the slow one earns only 0.6.

items.prose: About 5 seconds an event. Place each against a benchmark first.
items.question: Put the events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in four rolls
A total of 8 or more with two dice

feedback.correct: Four rolls 0.518, then 8 or more 0.417, then 4 or more heads 0.344.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each event’s rough size first.

byKey.eight: 8 or more is $\tfrac{15}{36} = 0.417$, below a half. Four rolls give $1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} = 0.518$.
byKey.heads: 4 or more heads in 6 is $\tfrac{22}{64} = 0.344$, the smallest.
byKey.four: Four rolls give 0.518, just above a half: first.

explain.text: Four rolls give $1 - (5/6)^4 = 0.518$, just over a half. A total of 8 or more is $\tfrac{15}{36} = 0.417$. Four or more heads in 6 is $\tfrac{15 + 6 + 1}{64} = 0.344$.

items.prose: Each of 20 independent trades loses with chance 5%.
items.question: What is the chance that at least one loses, to two decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the chance that none loses from 1.

byKey.np: $20 \times 0.05 = 1$ adds the overlaps. The chance is $1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.64$.
byKey.none: 0.36 is the chance that none loses. At least one is 0.64.

explain.text: Here $np = 1$, so the benchmark is $1 - 1/e = 0.63$. Exactly, $0.95^{20} = 0.358$ and at least one is 0.642. Either ranks it the same way.

items.prose: 10% of applicants are strong. A screen passes 80% of strong applicants and 20% of the rest.
items.question: An applicant passes. What is the chance they are strong?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture 1,000 applicants and count those who pass.

byKey.hit: 0.8 is passing given strong. You want strong given passing: 80 of 260.
byKey.joint: 0.08 is strong and passing out of all 1,000. Divide by the 260 who pass.

explain.text: Of 1,000, 100 are strong and 80 pass. Of 900 others, 180 pass. So 80 of 260 who pass are strong: $\tfrac{4}{13}$.

items.prose: Two cards are dealt from a full deck.
items.question: What is the chance both are hearts?

options.why: You used $\tfrac14$ twice, as if the first heart went back.
That is one heart. Both must be.
That is the second card alone. Multiply by $\tfrac{13}{52}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. After a heart, 12 hearts remain among 51.

byKey.rep: You used $\tfrac14$ twice, as if the first heart went back.
byKey.one: That is one heart. Both must be.
byKey.second: That is the second card alone. Multiply by $\tfrac{13}{52}$.

explain.text: First a heart: $\tfrac{13}{52} = \tfrac14$. Then 12 hearts among 51. Multiply: $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac{12}{51} = \tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{17}$.

widget.label: Next term
widget.accept: 16: the odd places go up by 4.

feedback.correct: 16: place 7 is odd, and 4, 8, 12 go up by 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split odd and even places.

explain.text: The odd places climb by 4 and the even places fall by 5. Place 7 is odd, so 16.

items.prose: About 30 seconds. Differences and ratios fail.
items.question: What comes next: 23, 28, 38, 49, 62, 70, ?

feedback.correct: 77: each term adds its digit sum, and $7 + 0 = 7$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each gap with the digits of the term before.

byKey.repeat-gap: You added the last gap, 8, again. Each gap is the digit sum of the term before: $70 + 7 = 77$.

explain.text: The gaps 5, 10, 11, 13, 8 are the digit sums of 23, 28, 38, 49 and 62. So 70 adds $7 + 0 = 7$: 77.

items.prose: A battery’s sequences section is reported as 12 items in 20 minutes.
items.question: What is the pace in seconds an item?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Seconds over items.

byKey.minutes: That is the pace in minutes. In seconds: 100.
byKey.ratio: That is items per minute. The pace is seconds per item.

explain.text: 20 minutes is 1,200 s; over 12 items that is 100 s each. Write it at the top of the section.

items.prose: A battery review. Probability, paced at 2 minutes: five wrong answers, each in under 50 s, and 4 minutes unused. Arithmetic, just before it: 19 right of 20.
items.question: What does the review point to?

options.text: The arithmetic pace carried into probability: slow to about 2 minutes
A probability method gap: drill the formulas
options.why: Method gaps are wrong answers after more than the pace. These came in under 50 s.
Five slips in one section, all fast, is a pattern, not luck.
Arithmetic went well, and probability had 4 minutes spare. Time was not short.

feedback.correct: A carried pace: fast, wrong and time to spare.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the seconds with the 2-minute pace.

byKey.method: Method gaps are wrong answers after more than the pace. These came in under 50 s.
byKey.luck: Five slips in one section, all fast, is a pattern, not luck.
byKey.arith: Arithmetic went well, and probability had 4 minutes spare. Time was not short.

explain.text: Fast wrong answers with time to spare mean the section ran on the wrong clock. The fix is the section’s own pace, written at its top. A method drill would not touch it.
